differentiation.title: Five reasons we use texts
differentiation.activity: Students examine five short, teacher-created texts: a narrative, an informational notice, a how-to explanation, an evaluation, and a proposal. They identify each text's primary purpose, highlight evidence supporting their decision, and compose a short example of one selected purpose.
differentiation.scaffolds: Purpose reference chart, short accessible examples, color-coded annotations, sentence frames, teacher modeling.
differentiation.success: Identify the primary purpose of at least four texts, support two classifications with evidence, and create a short text that fulfills an identified purpose.
differentiation.materials: Five short sample texts; purpose chart; annotation tools.

differentiation.title: One topic, three purposes
differentiation.activity: Students select a familiar school or community topic, such as school lunch, transportation, or recreational spaces. They read two short texts presenting relevant information. They then create three distinct communications: a brief narrative illustrating an experience, an explanation of the issue, and a recommendation supported by evidence. Students annotate how purpose influenced their choices.
differentiation.scaffolds: Text selection guide, three-purpose planning organizer, models of each form, peer feedback.
differentiation.success: Produce three clearly differentiated texts, use relevant information accurately, and explain at least three purposeful communication choices.
differentiation.materials: Two informational texts; planning organizer; writing document.

differentiation.title: From inquiry to impact
differentiation.activity: Students investigate a genuine school or community problem using multiple credible texts. They synthesize findings, evaluate proposed solutions, and create a communication package for a defined audience: a short explanatory brief, an evidence-based recommendation, and a narrative or visual element illustrating the human implications of the issue. Students present the package and reflect on the strengths and limitations of their evidence.
differentiation.scaffolds: Optional inquiry template, source evaluation checklist, audience planning guide, conferencing.
differentiation.success: Demonstrate accurate understanding, meaningful connections across sources, reasoned evaluation of alternatives, and a persuasive recommendation appropriate to the audience.
differentiation.materials: Credible sources; research organizer; presentation or publishing tools; evaluation rubric.

questions.prompt: A student reads several articles about local water quality and uses the findings to recommend a new testing procedure. Which purpose is most directly demonstrated?
options: Sharing an imagined experience
Solving a problem or influencing a decision
Recounting events for entertainment
Describing a character's motivation
questions.answer: Solving a problem or influencing a decision
questions.rationale: The student interprets information and constructs a recommendation intended to address a practical problem.

questions.prompt: Which task most directly demonstrates using texts to explain and learn a process?
options: Reading a procedural article and creating an illustrated guide that accurately explains its steps
Reading a short story and identifying the protagonist
Listing the titles of five favorite books
Memorizing the publication dates of several novels
questions.answer: Reading a procedural article and creating an illustrated guide that accurately explains its steps
questions.rationale: The task requires both interpretation and construction of explanatory texts focused on a process.

questions.prompt: A writer publishes a personal story about struggling to access public transportation, followed by factual information about transportation options. Explain two different purposes the combined text could serve.
questions.answer: The personal story may communicate an experience and help readers understand its human significance. The factual information may build knowledge, clarify the issue, or support informed decisions. A strong response explains how the two purposes reinforce one another.
questions.rationale: Assesses recognition of overlapping purposes within a single text.

questions.prompt: Read two short texts that address the same issue but reach different conclusions. Identify one point of agreement, one point of disagreement, and the evidence each author uses. Explain which conclusion is better supported and why.
questions.answer: A strong response accurately identifies the texts' positions, distinguishes agreement from disagreement, evaluates relevant evidence, and supports a reasoned judgment without relying solely on personal preference.
questions.rationale: Assesses interpretation and construction of analysis and evaluation, including connections between texts.

questions.prompt: Choose a school or community issue. Read at least three relevant texts representing different kinds of information or perspectives. Create a communication portfolio containing: a 150–200-word narrative illustrating an experience connected to the issue; a 200-word explanation of its causes, processes, or background; a 250-word analysis evaluating relevant evidence or possible responses; and a 200-word proposal recommending an informed action. Conclude with a reflection explaining how the texts informed your thinking and how your purpose changed across the four pieces.
questions.answer: Evaluate the accurate interpretation of sources, effectiveness of storytelling, clarity of explanation, quality of analysis, reasoning behind the proposed action, purposeful connections among texts, and the student's ability to adapt communication to different purposes.
questions.rationale: Integrates all five expectations through a coherent sequence of interpretation and construction tasks.

evidence: An annotated collection of texts identifying primary and secondary communicative purposes.
An original narrative communicating a real or imagined experience.
A knowledge-building response synthesizing information from a text.
An explanation of a concept or process for a defined audience.
An analytical or evaluative response supported by textual evidence.
A proposal addressing a problem or recommending a decision.
A comparative organizer documenting connections within, between, and beyond texts.
A reflection explaining how audience and purpose influenced choices during composition.
instruction: Introduce the standard by asking students what they want to accomplish when they read, write, speak, or listen.
Teach the five expectations as overlapping communicative purposes rather than rigid, mutually exclusive genres.
Use authentic examples showing how a single text may tell a story, explain an idea, and influence an audience.
Model the distinction between identifying a text's topic and identifying its purpose.
Provide paired interpretation and construction activities so students read with a purpose and then create something meaningful.
Use narrative as a means of communicating experience without assuming that every narrative must be autobiographical.
Teach students to distinguish explaining information from analyzing or evaluating its significance.
Provide real or realistic decision-making contexts that require students to consider evidence and alternatives.
Build text-to-text connections through comparison, synthesis, and discussion.
Extend text-to-world connections through relevant historical, scientific, cultural, or community contexts.
Offer varied modes of communication, including written, spoken, visual, and multimodal texts when appropriate.
Teach students to identify a specific audience and intended outcome before composing.
Use reflection prompts asking students how their purpose shaped selection, organization, evidence, and language.
Assess how successfully a text fulfills its purpose, not merely whether it follows a familiar format.
watchFor: Treating the five expectations as five fixed writing genres rather than purposes that can overlap.
Confusing the topic of a text with the reason it was created.
Assuming all stories exist only to entertain.
Equating knowledge-building with copying or listing facts.
Confusing explanation with unsupported opinion.
Treating analysis as summary without examination of relationships or significance.
Treating evaluation as personal preference without criteria or evidence.
Asking students to solve problems without supplying sufficient information or a realistic decision-making context.
Assuming that a persuasive text is effective simply because it expresses a strong opinion.
Making superficial text-to-world connections that do not deepen understanding.
Expecting students to construct effective texts without first examining examples.
Ignoring how audience and purpose affect the choice of form, detail, evidence, and language.
Requiring personal disclosure when an imagined narrative could demonstrate the same expectation.
Grading students primarily on whether they advocate a preferred solution rather than on the quality of their reasoning.
unpackings.readingSelectionNote: Selections are illustrative teacher-developed recommendations, not state-prescribed works. Confirm text access, permissions, excerpt length, and age suitability. High Interest and accessibility are editorial judgments rather than validated reading-level scores. Because this practice standard addresses multiple purposes and text types, teachers should supplement literary selections with authentic informational, explanatory, analytical, and problem-solving texts. Students should be assessed on the quality of interpretation and construction, not on agreement with a particular position.

unpackings.status: draft — independently developed instructional guidance; educator review recommended
unpackings.studentFriendly: I can investigate the historical, cultural, geographic, and social circumstances surrounding a text. I can explain how those circumstances influence an author's choices, an audience's response, and the way I interpret or create texts.
know: Context includes circumstances that surround the creation, circulation, interpretation, and reception of a text.
Historical context includes events, conditions, and ideas associated with a particular time period.
Geographic context includes locations and physical environments that may influence experiences and perspectives.
Cultural context includes traditions, values, languages, practices, and shared experiences that may influence communication.
Social and political circumstances can influence the issues writers address and the choices available to them.
Contemporary events can shape both the creation of new texts and the interpretation of older ones.
Authors and audiences may possess different knowledge, assumptions, experiences, and expectations.
Primary sources and credible secondary sources can provide useful contextual information.
Prior knowledge and discussion can generate contextual questions, but claims should be checked against reliable evidence.
Not every contextual detail is equally relevant to understanding a particular text.
Context can inform interpretation without determining a single correct meaning.
Writers make decisions about language, examples, references, and explanation based partly on the circumstances of their intended audiences.
understand: Texts emerge from particular circumstances rather than existing in isolation.
Relevant contextual knowledge can clarify references, conflicts, assumptions, and choices that readers might otherwise misunderstand.
Historical and cultural circumstances can influence an author's purposes without fully explaining every artistic or rhetorical decision.
Audiences from different times, places, and communities may interpret the same text differently.
Contextual investigation requires selecting information that meaningfully contributes to an interpretation.
Evidence from the text and evidence about its context should work together.
Writers can anticipate audience knowledge and provide necessary context to make their communications more effective.
Responsible contextual analysis avoids reducing individuals or communities to stereotypes.
New contextual knowledge may complicate or change an initial interpretation.
do: Activate relevant prior knowledge and identify questions about a text's circumstances (9.P.ST.1.a).
Use formal or informal research and discussion to investigate relevant historical, geographic, cultural, or contemporary context (9.P.ST.1.a).
Distinguish contextual information that meaningfully supports interpretation from background details that are merely interesting (9.P.ST.1.a).
Explain how context may influence an author's purpose or intended audience (9.P.ST.1.b).
Consider how different audiences' circumstances and expectations may influence their purposes for engaging with a text (9.P.ST.1.b).
Analyze relationships between context and an author's choices of subject, language, structure, examples, or emphasis (9.P.ST.1.c).
Explore how different audiences may respond to the same text because of differences in contextual knowledge or experience (9.P.ST.1.c).
Use contextual knowledge when constructing texts, including decisions about what background information an audience needs (9.P.ST.1.a–c).
Support contextual interpretations with relevant evidence from texts and credible contextual sources (9.P.ST.1.a–c).
targets: I can identify which aspects of context are important to understanding a text.
I can investigate a contextual question using credible sources or informed discussion.
I can explain how an event, location, or cultural circumstance relates to a text.
I can connect contextual information to a specific passage or authorial choice.
I can explain how context may influence an author's purpose.
I can compare how audiences from different circumstances might respond to a text.
I can revise my interpretation when new contextual evidence becomes available.
I can provide appropriate background information when writing for a particular audience.
I can distinguish evidence-based contextual analysis from unsupported assumptions.

vocabulary.definition: The circumstances surrounding the creation, content, interpretation, or reception of a text.
vocabulary.example: Understanding the conditions of the Great Depression may illuminate references in a novel set during that period.

vocabulary.definition: The events, conditions, beliefs, and circumstances associated with a particular period.
vocabulary.example: The American Civil War provides important context for interpreting the Gettysburg Address.

vocabulary.definition: The practices, values, languages, traditions, and experiences relevant to a text or its audience.
vocabulary.example: Knowledge of cultural traditions can help readers understand references in a memoir.

vocabulary.definition: The physical location and environmental circumstances relevant to a text.
vocabulary.example: A coastal community's geography may influence the conflicts described in a story.

vocabulary.definition: The social structures, relationships, institutions, and expectations relevant to communication.
vocabulary.example: Social expectations about gender may help explain a character's limited choices.

vocabulary.definition: The governmental conditions, power relationships, policies, and public debates relevant to a text.
vocabulary.example: A speech advocating voting rights responds to a particular political situation.

vocabulary.definition: Events occurring during a particular period, especially those relevant to the creation or interpretation of a text.
vocabulary.example: A recent natural disaster may shape the urgency of a community announcement.

vocabulary.definition: Original evidence or firsthand material from the period, event, or subject being investigated.
vocabulary.example: A contemporary newspaper article can provide evidence about how an event was reported at the time.

vocabulary.definition: A source that analyzes, interprets, or explains information drawn from other evidence.
vocabulary.example: A historian's scholarly article analyzes the circumstances surrounding a historical speech.

vocabulary.definition: The people a text was originally designed to reach.
vocabulary.example: A public letter may address named critics while also appealing to a wider readership.

vocabulary.definition: The ways audiences respond to or interpret a text.
vocabulary.example: A novel may receive different responses when it is published and when it is studied decades later.

vocabulary.definition: A decision an author makes about a text's content, form, language, or presentation.
vocabulary.example: A writer includes a familiar historical reference to establish common ground with an audience.

vocabulary.definition: The tendency to interpret the past primarily through present-day assumptions or values without adequately considering historical circumstances.
vocabulary.example: A reader overlooks the limitations of a historical character's circumstances when judging every choice solely by modern expectations.

differentiation.title: Three clues to context
differentiation.activity: Students read a short literary passage and examine three teacher-selected contextual sources: a brief timeline, an image or map, and a short explanatory paragraph. They identify which source provides the most relevant information for understanding a specific textual detail. Students then explain the connection using a sentence frame.
differentiation.scaffolds: Short accessible passage, curated sources, visual timeline, color-coded evidence, modeled explanation.
differentiation.success: Identify two relevant contextual facts and accurately connect each to a detail in the text.
differentiation.materials: Literary excerpt; timeline; map or image; short contextual source; response organizer.

differentiation.title: Read it twice

differentiation.scaffolds: Contextual source packet, before-and-after organizer, teacher model distinguishing evidence from inference, partner discussion.

differentiation.title: One text, multiple audiences
differentiation.activity: Students investigate the original circumstances and reception of a historical speech, literary work, or public argument. They identify its intended audience and research at least one later audience or interpretive context. Students compose a comparative analysis explaining how circumstances may influence purpose, authorial choices, and audience responses. They then write a short introduction designed to provide essential context to a contemporary reader.
differentiation.scaffolds: Optional source evaluation guide, contextual research planner, analytical writing model, individual conference.
differentiation.success: Use credible evidence to explain relevant context, distinguish supported conclusions from speculation, compare audience responses, and provide an effective contextual introduction.
differentiation.materials: Selected text; primary and secondary sources; research organizer; writing document.

questions.prompt: A student is studying the Gettysburg Address. Which information would be most directly relevant to interpreting the speech's immediate purpose?
options: The history of printing technology in the eighteenth century
The Civil War and the dedication ceremony at which Lincoln delivered the speech
The architectural design of the modern Lincoln Memorial
The number of American presidents who served after Lincoln
questions.answer: The Civil War and the dedication ceremony at which Lincoln delivered the speech
questions.rationale: The speech's historical circumstances and occasion directly inform its purpose and intended audience.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains the relationship between context and interpretation?
options: Context always determines one correct interpretation of a text.
Context is useful only when a text contains unfamiliar vocabulary.
Relevant context can deepen or complicate an interpretation when connected to textual evidence.
Modern readers should ignore historical circumstances when evaluating older texts.
questions.answer: Relevant context can deepen or complicate an interpretation when connected to textual evidence.
questions.rationale: Context informs interpretation but does not replace close reading or eliminate reasonable differences among readers.

questions.prompt: A novel was published during a period of major social change. Explain how researching that period might help you understand the author's choices. Identify one type of contextual source you would consult.
questions.answer: A strong response identifies a specific possible relationship between social circumstances and an author's subject, language, characterization, or purpose. It proposes an appropriate contextual source and avoids claiming that historical circumstances automatically explain the author's intentions.
questions.rationale: Assesses selection of relevant context and reasoning about its relationship to authorial decisions.

questions.prompt: A speech delivered to a local community during a crisis is republished decades later for students studying history. Explain how the purposes and responses of the original audience and the later student audience might differ.
questions.answer: The original audience may have sought guidance, reassurance, or immediate action, while the later audience may seek historical understanding or rhetorical analysis. A strong response connects these possibilities to the audiences' circumstances and recognizes that individual responses can vary.
questions.rationale: Assesses consideration of how context influences audience purposes and responses.

questions.prompt: Select a literary, historical, or rhetorical text for which relevant contextual sources are available. Investigate at least three contextual factors, such as time period, location, cultural circumstances, or contemporary events. Write a 350–500-word analysis explaining which factors are most relevant, how they may have influenced the author's purpose and decisions, and how audiences in different circumstances might respond. Support the analysis with textual evidence and credible contextual sources. Then compose a 150-word introduction that provides essential context for a new audience.
questions.answer: Evaluate the relevance and accuracy of contextual research, the distinction between evidence and inference, the explanation of relationships among context, purpose, authorial choices, and audience responses, and the effectiveness of the contextual introduction.
questions.rationale: Integrates contextual investigation, interpretation of author and audience purposes, and purposeful construction for a defined audience.

evidence: A contextual inquiry chart identifying relevant questions and credible sources.
An annotated text connecting contextual information to specific passages.

differentiation.title: Who is this for?
differentiation.activity: Students examine three short communications about the same topic: a message to students, a formal report for administrators, and a family-facing announcement. differentiation.title: The audience shift

differentiation.scaffolds: Rhetorical analysis organizer, audience profiles, model adaptation, peer feedback.

questions.prompt: A school publishes instructions for incoming ninth-grade students selecting their first high school courses. Which design decision best serves the intended audience?
options: Use unexplained abbreviations because school employees already know them.
Present every district policy in one uninterrupted paragraph.
Organize instructions into clearly labeled steps and explain unfamiliar terms.
Place the most important deadlines in an unrelated document without a link.
questions.answer: Organize instructions into clearly labeled steps and explain unfamiliar terms.
questions.rationale: The design anticipates the audience's limited prior knowledge and makes the required information easier to understand and use.

questions.prompt: Which question is most useful when evaluating whether an author has achieved a text's purpose?
options: Does the text contain at least five paragraphs?
Would every possible reader agree with the author?
How do the text's evidence, language, and design support its intended outcome for its audience?
Does the author use the longest words available?
questions.answer: How do the text's evidence, language, and design support its intended outcome for its audience?
questions.rationale: Evaluating effectiveness requires examining the relationship among purpose, audience, and the author's choices.

questions.prompt: Two writers discuss the same proposed school policy. One is a student affected by the policy, and the other is an administrator responsible for implementing it. Explain how their perspectives might influence which information they emphasize. Avoid assuming that either perspective is automatically more accurate.
questions.answer: A strong response explains that a student may emphasize everyday experiences and consequences, while an administrator may emphasize implementation, resources, or institutional responsibilities. The response recognizes that individual authors can differ and that claims still require evidence.
questions.rationale: Assesses understanding of how authorial perspective can shape content and emphasis.

questions.prompt: Revise this announcement for students who have never attended a high school club meeting: 'All interested parties should report to the designated venue for organizational proceedings.' Explain how your revision better serves the audience.
questions.answer: One appropriate revision is: 'Interested in joining the club? Come to our first meeting in Room 214 on Thursday after school.' The revision uses familiar language and a welcoming tone. The room and time are illustrative details that would need to be verified in an actual announcement.
questions.rationale: Assesses audience awareness and purposeful selection of accessible language and relevant information.

questions.prompt: Choose a school or community topic that requires communication with two different audiences. Research each audience's likely needs and existing knowledge. Create two texts of 250–350 words each, or equivalent multimodal products, addressing the same core subject from a consistent, clearly established perspective. Adapt the information, organization, diction, syntax, and design for each audience. Write a 300-word commentary comparing the choices and evaluating how effectively each product fulfills its purpose.
questions.answer: Evaluate the clarity of audience and purpose, consistency and appropriateness of perspective, relevance of selected information, accessibility of design, effectiveness of diction and syntax, and the quality of the student's explanation and evaluation.
questions.rationale: Integrates interpretation and construction across the three expectations through authentic audience-based composition and rhetorical analysis.

differentiation.title: Notice, name, explain

differentiation.title: The craft experiment

questions.prompt: A suspense writer follows a long descriptive paragraph with the sentence 'The door opened.' What is the most plausible effect of this change in syntax?
options: It necessarily makes the narrator unreliable.
It can create a sudden moment of emphasis and interrupt the previous rhythm.
It removes the need for descriptive details.
It guarantees that readers will understand the ending.
questions.answer: It can create a sudden moment of emphasis and interrupt the previous rhythm.
questions.rationale: A short sentence can stand out against longer surrounding sentences, changing rhythm and directing attention.

questions.prompt: Which response best demonstrates reading like a writer?
options: The story is about a person who becomes frightened.
The story was interesting and easy to understand.
The author repeats the same phrase as the character becomes increasingly anxious, creating a sense of mounting pressure.
The main character makes an important decision near the end.
questions.answer: The author repeats the same phrase as the character becomes increasingly anxious, creating a sense of mounting pressure.
questions.rationale: The response identifies a specific craft technique and explains its contribution to the reader's experience.

questions.prompt: A digital guide has attractive illustrations but uses vague headings, unlabeled links, and long unbroken paragraphs. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
options: The illustrations guarantee that the guide is accessible.
The guide's visual appeal eliminates the need for organization.
The design may hinder navigation and understanding despite its attractive appearance.
Text design has no relationship to the author's purpose.
questions.answer: The design may hinder navigation and understanding despite its attractive appearance.
questions.rationale: Effective design considers usability, accessibility, audience needs, and purpose, not visual attractiveness alone.

questions.prompt: Read this original passage: 'The hallway stretched ahead. Silent. Empty. Then came the footsteps.' Explain how the sentence structure and diction contribute to the passage's effect. Suggest one revision that would change the pacing.
questions.answer: A strong response explains that fragments and short sentences isolate details and may create suspense. Words such as 'silent' and 'empty' emphasize absence. A valid revision might combine sentences into a longer descriptive sentence to create a smoother, slower rhythm, with an explanation of the changed effect.
questions.rationale: Assesses analysis of diction and syntax together with the ability to make purposeful revisions.

questions.prompt: Select a 200–350-word literary, expository, or rhetorical mentor passage. Identify and analyze four craft choices: one literary, expository, or rhetorical element; one example of diction; one syntactic decision; and one organizational or design feature. Explain how each affects the intended audience and supports the text's purpose. Then construct a 350–500-word original text, or equivalent multimodal product, applying at least three of the techniques for a clearly defined audience. Submit a 250-word commentary explaining your choices and evaluating their effectiveness.
questions.answer: Evaluate accuracy and specificity of craft analysis, attention to audience and purpose, appropriate use of textual evidence, purposeful application of techniques, consideration of organization and accessibility, and quality of reflection.
questions.rationale: Integrates all four expectations through analysis, application, evaluation, and reflection.

evidence: An annotated mentor text identifying literary, expository, or rhetorical techniques and their effects.

instruction: Begin craft study with an authentic reader response: surprise, confusion, tension, curiosity, admiration, or another noticeable effect.
Ask students to investigate which specific authorial decisions may have produced that response.
Model the difference between identifying a technique and analyzing its function.
Use the recurring questions: What did the author do? How does it work? Why might it matter for this audience and purpose?
Select short mentor passages with craft choices students can clearly observe and experiment with.
Teach literary, expository, and rhetorical techniques across genres rather than limiting craft study to fiction.
Include diction and syntax in close-reading lessons, not only in grammar instruction.
Use imitation exercises that preserve the function of a technique while allowing students to create original content.
Compare original and revised passages to make the effects of craft choices visible.
Study organization and design in both print and digital texts.
Include accessibility considerations when evaluating digital and multimodal compositions.
Ask students to explain why a technique works in its particular context rather than labeling it universally effective.
Provide opportunities to revise original writing based on craft analysis and audience feedback.
Assess the quality of explanation and application rather than the number of literary terms students can identify.
watchFor: Reducing reading like a writer to highlighting literary devices.
Assuming that naming a technique constitutes analysis.
Treating every use of a technique as equally effective.
Claiming certainty about an author's intention without supporting evidence.
Ignoring the relationship between craft, audience, and purpose.
Discussing diction without examining the significance of particular words.
Treating syntax only as grammatical correctness rather than a resource for meaning and effect.
Assuming short sentences always create suspense or long sentences always slow pacing.
Confusing a reader's personal reaction with an effect that every reader must experience.
Using imitation exercises that reproduce copyrighted passages rather than developing original writing.
Evaluating digital design solely by its appearance.
Overlooking how headings, spacing, structure, and navigation affect accessibility.
Requiring students to use sophisticated techniques when simpler choices better serve their purpose.
Separating craft analysis from opportunities to write and revise.
Rewarding terminology more than precise observation and evidence-based explanation.

vocabulary.definition: The process through which an audience encounters, understands, and responds to a text.

vocabulary.definition: An intentional choice about content, language, structure, technique, or design.

vocabulary.definition: A method used to develop meaning or effect in literary writing.

vocabulary.definition: A method used to clarify, explain, or develop information.

vocabulary.definition: A communicative strategy intended to influence understanding, judgment, or action.

vocabulary.definition: The purposeful selection of words and phrases.

vocabulary.definition: The rate at which information, ideas, or events unfold for an audience.

vocabulary.definition: The process of predicting what readers may expect, question, or need.
vocabulary.example: A guide answers a likely question before readers reach a complicated step.

vocabulary.definition: The arrangement and relationships of a text's parts.
vocabulary.example: A proposal moves from the problem to evidence, alternatives, and a recommendation.

vocabulary.definition: The degree to which people can perceive, navigate, understand, and use a text.

vocabulary.definition: Information from an audience about how a text is understood or experienced.
vocabulary.example: A peer explains where an instruction was unclear or where an argument raised an unanswered question.

differentiation.title: What will my reader need?
differentiation.activity: Students receive a short, deliberately unclear set of instructions for a familiar classroom task. They identify three likely reader questions, revise confusing words and sentences, and reorganize the instructions into clearly labeled steps. Partners test whether the revised directions are understandable.
differentiation.scaffolds: Audience question cards, teacher think-aloud, sentence-combining and splitting models, numbered-step template.
differentiation.success: Identify three reader needs and make at least three purposeful changes to wording, syntax, or organization.
differentiation.materials: Teacher-created instructions; audience checklist; revision organizer.

differentiation.title: Write for a reaction
differentiation.activity: Students select one intended audience response, such as curiosity, concern, suspense, confidence, or reconsideration. They examine a short mentor passage that produces a related effect, then write a 250-word original text using purposeful diction, syntax, and at least one literary, expository, or rhetorical technique. Peers describe their actual responses without first being told the writer's intention. Writers compare the feedback with their goals and revise.
differentiation.scaffolds: Mentor-text examples, reader-response planning chart, craft menu, structured feedback protocol.
differentiation.success: Demonstrate three intentional craft decisions, gather specific audience feedback, and justify at least two revisions.
differentiation.materials: Mentor passages; writing document; feedback and revision form.

differentiation.title: Engineer the reader's journey
differentiation.activity: Students design a 500–700-word feature article, persuasive essay, narrative, or equivalent multimodal publication for a defined audience. They map what readers should know, feel, question, or decide at several points in the text. They then select techniques, diction, syntax, organization, and accessible design features to support that progression. After testing a draft with representative readers, students revise and submit an annotated explanation of their decisions.
differentiation.scaffolds: Optional audience journey map, mentor-text comparison, accessibility checklist, writing conference.
differentiation.success: Create a coherent audience-centered text, apply multiple effective craft choices, respond thoughtfully to feedback, and evaluate whether the intended reader experience was achieved.
differentiation.materials: Audience journey organizer; mentor texts; publishing tools; peer response protocol; rubric.

questions.prompt: A student is writing an article explaining a complicated school scheduling process to incoming ninth graders. Which decision best demonstrates writing like a reader?
options: Use technical abbreviations without explanation.
Begin with the most complicated exception to the policy.
Introduce essential terms, organize the process into steps, and answer likely questions.
Assume readers already understand how high school schedules work.
questions.answer: Introduce essential terms, organize the process into steps, and answer likely questions.
questions.rationale: The choice anticipates the audience's knowledge and needs while using language and organization to support understanding.

questions.prompt: A writer wants to create a sudden moment of alarm after several paragraphs of calm description. Which revision is most likely to support that effect?
options: Insert a brief, direct sentence revealing the danger.
Add an unrelated explanation of the setting's history.
Replace every verb with a more complicated synonym.
Repeat the same descriptive paragraph.
questions.answer: Insert a brief, direct sentence revealing the danger.
questions.rationale: A sudden change in syntax and information can interrupt the established rhythm and direct readers' attention.

questions.prompt: A student creates a digital article with strong arguments but no headings, vague links, and an important chart without an explanation. Which revision best addresses audience experience?
options: Add decorative graphics without changing the content.
Use meaningful headings and links and provide an accessible explanation of the chart.
Remove all evidence to make the article shorter.
Increase the complexity of the vocabulary.
questions.answer: Use meaningful headings and links and provide an accessible explanation of the chart.
questions.rationale: Accessible organizational and design features help readers navigate and understand the text.

questions.prompt: A writer wants readers to question whether a character can be trusted. Describe two specific craft choices the writer could make, using different techniques, and explain the intended effect of each.
questions.answer: A strong response might suggest including inconsistencies between the character's statements and actions, using carefully selected details that contradict the character's claims, or controlling when readers discover important information. Each choice should be linked to the audience's developing uncertainty.
questions.rationale: Assesses the ability to select and justify techniques based on a planned reader response.

questions.prompt: Revise this original opening for an audience of students who have never participated in a research project: 'The utilization of authoritative repositories facilitates the acquisition of substantiated informational resources.' Explain at least three choices you make to improve the reader's experience.
questions.answer: One possible revision is: 'Start your research with reliable sources, such as library databases. These can help you find information supported by evidence.' A strong explanation addresses more familiar diction, clearer syntax, and an example that helps the audience understand the process.
questions.rationale: Assesses audience-centered revision of diction, syntax, and explanation.

questions.prompt: Create a 500–700-word original text, or equivalent multimodal product, for a clearly defined audience and purpose. Before drafting, develop a reader-experience map identifying what you want the audience to understand, feel, question, or decide at the beginning, middle, and end. Apply at least one literary, expository, or rhetorical technique, three deliberate diction choices, two purposeful syntactic decisions, and an organizational or design feature supporting accessibility. Obtain feedback from at least two readers, revise the text, and submit a 250-word commentary evaluating the relationship between your intentions, readers' actual responses, and your final craft choices.
questions.answer: Evaluate the appropriateness of techniques for audience and purpose, effectiveness of language and syntax, clarity and accessibility of organization, evidence of meaningful revision, and the precision of the student's reflection. Do not require readers to report identical emotional responses.
questions.rationale: Integrates all four expectations through planning, construction, audience feedback, and evaluation.

differentiation.title: Same information, different design
differentiation.activity: Students compare a short paragraph explaining a process with a labeled diagram and a numbered instruction sheet covering the same information. They identify the mode, genre, and useful features of each. They then reorganize a short paragraph into a clearly labeled sequence of steps.
differentiation.scaffolds: Teacher-created examples, visual comparison chart, limited feature vocabulary, model transformation.
differentiation.success: Identify at least three meaningful design differences and explain how two affect an audience's understanding.
differentiation.materials: Paragraph, diagram, instructions, comparison organizer.

differentiation.title: Remix the message
differentiation.activity: Students select an informational article and transform its central ideas into an infographic, a short audio script with accompanying visual plan, or a digital guide. They decide what information to preserve, condense, emphasize, or reorganize. Students then explain how the new mode and genre shaped those choices.
differentiation.scaffolds: Information-selection organizer, genre examples, design checklist, peer feedback.
differentiation.success: Preserve factual accuracy, select an appropriate structure, integrate meaningful features, and justify at least three design decisions.
differentiation.materials: Source article, storyboard or layout template, composition tools.

differentiation.title: Design a multimodal information experience
differentiation.activity: Students identify an authentic information need among high school students, such as understanding graduation requirements, locating research databases, or navigating an application process. They evaluate two existing examples, interview or survey a small number of potential users when feasible, and develop a multimodal guide combining written information with purposeful visual or audio elements. They test its usability and revise the design.
differentiation.scaffolds: Optional audience-research protocol, design planning sheet, accessibility checklist, feedback conference.
differentiation.success: Produce an accurate, coherent, accessible multimodal resource whose genre, information selection, organization, and features serve a clearly defined audience and purpose.
differentiation.materials: Credible sources, design or publishing tools, usability checklist, rubric.

questions.prompt: Students need to understand how three bus routes connect across a city. Which format would most directly communicate the geographic relationships?
options: A paragraph listing unrelated facts about transportation
A labeled route map with a clear legend
A poem describing the experience of riding a bus
A photograph without labels or context
questions.answer: A labeled route map with a clear legend
questions.rationale: A spatial representation is well suited to showing route locations and connections, while labels and a legend help audiences interpret the information.

questions.prompt: A student adapts a detailed research article into an infographic. Which decision best demonstrates understanding of genre?
options: Copy every paragraph into small text boxes.
Remove source information because visuals never need evidence.
Select the most relevant findings and present them through clearly labeled visual comparisons.
Use as many decorative images as possible.
questions.answer: Select the most relevant findings and present them through clearly labeled visual comparisons.
questions.rationale: The student adjusts information selection and arrangement to suit the genre while retaining meaningful content.

questions.prompt: Which example most clearly demonstrates purposeful multimodal composition?
options: A presentation with unrelated background music and decorative animations
A video that combines accurate narration, labeled diagrams, and captions to explain a process
An essay with randomly selected photographs
A poster using multiple fonts but providing no essential information
questions.answer: A video that combines accurate narration, labeled diagrams, and captions to explain a process
questions.rationale: The different modes work together to communicate information, support understanding, and improve access.

questions.prompt: A written transcript and a video recording present the same public speech. Identify two differences in how audiences may experience the versions and explain how those differences influence meaning or interpretation.
questions.answer: A strong response might discuss vocal emphasis, pauses, gestures, facial expression, pacing, or audience reaction in the recording, compared with the transcript's opportunities for rereading, annotation, and searching. Each difference should be linked to a specific interpretive effect.
questions.rationale: Assesses analysis of how mode and features influence meaning and audience experience.

questions.prompt: Compare an informational article and an infographic addressing the same topic. Explain one important difference in information selection, one difference in organization, and one advantage or limitation of each format for its intended audience.
questions.answer: A strong response identifies concrete examples, explains how genre influences content and arrangement, and evaluates the formats in relation to purpose rather than assuming one is universally superior.
questions.rationale: Assesses understanding of genre-based information selection and organization.

questions.prompt: Choose a topic relevant to students and investigate it using at least three credible sources. Create two products communicating the same essential information in different genres or modes. At least one must be multimodal. For example, produce a 400-word explanatory article and an infographic, or a digital guide and a short captioned video. Include accurate source attribution and accessible design features. Write a 300-word design commentary comparing the information selected, organizational decisions, specific features, and intended effects of the two products.
questions.answer: Evaluate factual accuracy, genre and mode awareness, purposeful information selection, appropriate organization, effective integration of multimodal elements, accessibility, and the student's ability to explain design decisions in relation to audience and purpose.
questions.rationale: Integrates all four expectations through comparative interpretation, text construction, multimodal design, and reflection.

evidence: A comparison chart identifying the modes, genres, and characteristic features of several texts.
An annotated text explaining how design features influence meaning, tone, style, or purpose.
An analysis comparing information selection across two genres.
A structural comparison explaining how different formats organize similar information.
A storyboard or wireframe for an original multimodal text.
An original infographic, digital guide, podcast, video, or other purposeful multimodal product.
An accessibility review documenting meaningful design choices.
A revision record showing changes made after audience or usability feedback.
A design commentary explaining how mode and genre shaped content and organization.
instruction: Introduce text design by comparing two authentic texts addressing the same subject through different modes or genres.
Teach mode and genre as related but distinct concepts.
Ask students what a chosen format makes easier or harder to communicate.
Analyze information selection before examining visual appearance.
Model how genre conventions influence the sequence and arrangement of ideas.
Examine how headings, captions, charts, diagrams, audio, and navigation features contribute to meaning.
Use graphic novels, recorded speeches, informational websites, maps, and data visualizations alongside conventional prose.
Teach students to evaluate the relationship between visual evidence and accompanying explanations.
Provide opportunities to transform a text from one mode or genre into another.
Require students to preserve accuracy when condensing or adapting source material.
Use storyboards and wireframes to plan multimodal texts before production.
Teach relevant accessibility practices, including captions, meaningful headings, readable contrast, descriptive links, and alternatives to essential visual information.
Include authentic audiences and purposes whenever possible.
Use peer feedback and usability testing to identify confusion or design barriers.
Assess the effectiveness of communication rather than the sophistication of the software used.
watchFor: Confusing mode with genre.
Treating text design as decoration rather than meaning-making.
Assuming multimodal means simply adding a picture to an essay.
Assuming every digital text is automatically multimodal.
Focusing on visual attractiveness while neglecting accuracy or purpose.
Copying all information from one genre into another without considering selection and arrangement.
Using charts or images without explaining what they represent.
Allowing decorative elements to compete with essential information.
Using color as the only means of communicating a distinction.
Using vague hyperlinks or unclear navigation.
Presenting data without sources, labels, units, or necessary context.
Assuming that fewer words always improve communication.
Treating genre conventions as inflexible rules.
Evaluating multimodal projects primarily by production quality rather than communication effectiveness.
Ignoring the needs of audiences who cannot access particular visual or audio elements.
Failing to consider whether the chosen mode and genre are appropriate for the intended audience.
unpackings.readingSelectionNote: Selections are illustrative teacher-developed recommendations, not state-prescribed works. Confirm access, permissions, excerpt length, and age suitability. High Interest and accessibility are editorial judgments rather than validated reading-level measures. Include both literary and functional multimodal texts so students experience how mode and genre shape communication across contexts. When evaluating or constructing multimodal work, prioritize meaning, accuracy, accessibility, and audience needs over decorative complexity.

unpackings.status: draft — independently developed instructional guidance; educator review recommended
unpackings.studentFriendly: I can prepare for discussions and group projects, work with others to set goals and expectations, contribute thoughtful ideas, listen and respond to different perspectives, and help my group investigate questions, solve problems, and create meaningful work.
know: Collaboration involves working with others toward a shared goal or product.
Preparation may include reading assigned texts, researching a question, developing ideas, and bringing relevant evidence.
Group norms establish expectations for participation, communication, respect, and accountability.
Shared goals identify what a group intends to accomplish.
Procedures help a group organize tasks, make decisions, manage time, and monitor progress.
Productive collaboration requires both contributing ideas and considering the ideas of others.
Active listening involves attending to another person's meaning and responding accurately.
Constructive feedback is specific, relevant, respectful, and directed toward improvement.
Questions can clarify ideas, deepen inquiry, reveal assumptions, and move a discussion forward.
Disagreement can strengthen collaborative thinking when participants use evidence and respectful reasoning.
Collaborative inquiry involves investigating questions through discussion, research, and shared analysis.
Shared projects require coordination and accountability, but equitable contribution does not always mean identical tasks.
Groups can collaborate to interpret texts, construct texts, evaluate information, and solve authentic problems.
Reflection helps collaborators evaluate both the quality of the work and the effectiveness of their process.
understand: Successful collaboration requires intentional preparation and participation.
Group norms and procedures can improve both productivity and the quality of discussion.
Collaboration is more than dividing work into separate pieces; it involves developing understanding together.
Listening and responding thoughtfully are intellectual contributions.
Differences in perspective can lead to stronger interpretations and solutions.
Evidence-based disagreement can advance a group's thinking without becoming personal conflict.
Clear goals and accountability help groups manage complex tasks.
Effective collaborators adjust their roles and approaches to support shared progress.
Feedback is most useful when it provides a specific basis for revision or reconsideration.
A successful group product does not necessarily demonstrate that every member participated meaningfully.
Collaborative skills can be learned, practiced, observed, and improved.
do: Prepare for discussions and meetings by completing assigned reading, gathering evidence, and developing relevant questions or ideas (9.P.CP.1.a).
Participate actively and purposefully in group discussions and collaborative meetings (9.P.CP.1.a).
Work with peers to establish and apply group norms, shared goals, and procedures (9.P.CP.1.b).
Use collaborative planning and progress monitoring to support productive shared work (9.P.CP.1.b).
Contribute ideas and relevant evidence during discussions and projects (9.P.CP.1.c).
Listen accurately to others, acknowledge contributions, and respond to their ideas (9.P.CP.1.c).
Provide and respond to specific, constructive feedback (9.P.CP.1.c).
Collaborate to explore and interpret literary, informational, and multimodal texts (9.P.CP.1.d).
Investigate questions and evaluate possible solutions through shared inquiry (9.P.CP.1.d).
Plan, draft, revise, or produce texts collaboratively while maintaining a coherent shared purpose (9.P.CP.1.d).
Reflect on individual contributions, group processes, and the quality of collaborative outcomes (9.P.CP.1.a–d).
targets: I can arrive at a discussion with relevant preparation and evidence.
I can help my group establish clear goals and workable norms.
I can participate in decisions about roles, procedures, and deadlines.
I can contribute ideas that advance the group's thinking.
I can listen carefully and accurately summarize another person's idea.
I can ask questions that clarify or deepen discussion.
I can disagree respectfully and support my reasoning with evidence.
I can give useful feedback and respond constructively to feedback I receive.
I can work with others to investigate questions and solve problems.
I can help create a coherent shared text or project.
I can evaluate my own contribution and suggest improvements to our collaboration.

vocabulary.example: Students jointly investigate a literary question and construct an evidence-based interpretation.

vocabulary.definition: Shared expectations that guide participation, communication, and accountability.
vocabulary.example: Group members agree to invite contributions, cite evidence, and respond respectfully.

vocabulary.definition: An outcome that members of a group work toward together.
vocabulary.example: A group aims to produce a well-supported comparison of two poems.

vocabulary.definition: An agreed-upon process for organizing or completing collaborative work.
vocabulary.example: A group begins meetings by reviewing progress and ends by assigning next steps.

vocabulary.definition: Responsibility for fulfilling commitments and contributing to shared progress.
vocabulary.example: Each member completes an agreed research task and explains the findings to the group.

vocabulary.definition: Attentive listening that seeks to understand and respond meaningfully to another person's ideas.
vocabulary.example: A student paraphrases a peer's interpretation before offering a different reading.

vocabulary.definition: Specific observations and suggestions intended to improve thinking, communication, or work.
vocabulary.example: A peer identifies an unsupported claim and suggests where additional evidence is needed.

vocabulary.definition: A shared investigation in which participants develop questions, examine evidence, and construct understanding.
vocabulary.example: A group researches how a historical event influenced several literary works.

vocabulary.definition: A decision or position that group members can support after considering relevant ideas and concerns.
vocabulary.example: After evaluating alternatives, a group agrees on the strongest interpretation.

vocabulary.definition: A conversation in which claims and interpretations are supported by relevant information.
vocabulary.example: Students refer to specific passages when debating a character's motivation.

vocabulary.definition: The practice of helping a group communicate, remain focused, and make progress.
vocabulary.example: A facilitator invites quieter participants to contribute and redirects an off-topic conversation.

vocabulary.definition: The integration of multiple ideas or sources into a coherent understanding.
vocabulary.example: A group combines several interpretations into a nuanced explanation.

vocabulary.definition: A process in which peers examine work and provide feedback for improvement.
vocabulary.example: Students exchange draft editorials and offer evidence-based revision suggestions.

vocabulary.definition: Thoughtful evaluation of experiences, decisions, processes, or outcomes.
vocabulary.example: A student identifies which discussion strategy helped the group resolve a disagreement.

differentiation.title: Prepared, heard, and included
differentiation.activity: Students read a short passage independently and record one interpretation, one piece of evidence, and one question. In groups of three, they establish two discussion norms and use a structured round-robin to share ideas. Each student must accurately paraphrase a peer's contribution before adding a new idea. The group creates a two-sentence interpretation reflecting its discussion.
differentiation.scaffolds: Short accessible passage, preparation organizer, discussion stems, assigned turn-taking, teacher modeling.
differentiation.success: Arrive with prepared evidence, contribute an idea, accurately acknowledge another contribution, and help produce a shared interpretation.
differentiation.materials: Short text; discussion organizer; group norms card; shared response sheet.

differentiation.title: Literary inquiry team
differentiation.activity: Groups of four investigate a debatable interpretive question about a shared literary text. Students prepare individual claims and evidence before meeting. Each group establishes norms, assigns flexible responsibilities, examines competing interpretations, and produces a collaborative analytical paragraph or discussion brief. Students provide peer feedback and complete an individual reflection.
differentiation.scaffolds: Inquiry question bank, evidence organizer, discussion protocol, collaborative writing template, peer feedback guide.
differentiation.success: Demonstrate preparation, meaningful contribution, evidence-based dialogue, constructive feedback, and a coherent group product.
differentiation.materials: Shared literary text; discussion organizer; collaborative writing document; reflection form.

differentiation.title: Student editorial collective
differentiation.activity: Students form an editorial team to create a themed literary or cultural publication. They establish an editorial mission, selection criteria, group norms, deadlines, and a decision-making process. Members solicit or create original pieces, evaluate submissions, provide revision feedback, fact-check relevant claims, and collaboratively design a publication. Each student maintains a contribution log and submits an individual reflection on the group's decisions and process.
differentiation.scaffolds: Optional editorial charter, project timeline, submission rubric, publication template, teacher conferences.
differentiation.success: Produce a coherent publication through documented collaborative inquiry, responsible decision-making, constructive feedback, and equitable participation.
differentiation.materials: Editorial planning documents; submission and feedback forms; shared publishing tools; contribution logs.

questions.prompt: A group will discuss whether a character's final decision was justified. Which student is best prepared to participate?
options: A student who plans to read the story after the discussion
A student who brings a claim, relevant textual evidence, and a question about an alternative interpretation
A student who has already decided that no other interpretation is acceptable
A student who intends to let classmates complete the discussion
questions.answer: A student who brings a claim, relevant textual evidence, and a question about an alternative interpretation
questions.rationale: Preparation includes developing ideas, gathering relevant evidence, and considering questions that support active discussion.

questions.prompt: A group project is falling behind because members disagree about responsibilities. What is the most productive next step?
options: Allow the loudest member to make every decision.
Stop discussing the project until the deadline.
Revisit the shared goal, clarify responsibilities, and agree on a workable procedure for monitoring progress.
Assign all remaining work to the fastest writer.
questions.answer: Revisit the shared goal, clarify responsibilities, and agree on a workable procedure for monitoring progress.
questions.rationale: Effective collaboration requires shared goals, agreed procedures, and attention to productivity.

questions.prompt: During a discussion, a classmate presents an interpretation you disagree with. Which response best supports collaborative inquiry?
options: That interpretation is obviously wrong.
I hear your point about the character's fear. How do you interpret the passage where the character chooses to return?
We should stop discussing this because we disagree.
My interpretation is correct because I spoke first.
questions.answer: I hear your point about the character's fear. How do you interpret the passage where the character chooses to return?
questions.rationale: The response acknowledges the other person's idea, introduces textual evidence, and invites further reasoning.

questions.prompt: A group of four students produces a strong presentation, but one member completed almost all the research and writing. Explain why the final product alone is insufficient evidence of effective collaboration. Recommend two changes to the group's process.
questions.answer: A strong response recognizes that the quality of a product does not establish whether members prepared, participated, or shared responsibility. Improvements might include agreed roles, progress checkpoints, individual preparation records, rotating responsibilities, or structured opportunities for each member to contribute.
questions.rationale: Assesses understanding of collaborative norms, accountability, and shared procedures.

questions.prompt: Read a short scene from a play in which several characters must make a collective decision. Identify one behavior that improves the group's reasoning and one that undermines it. Explain each effect using evidence from the scene, then propose a discussion norm that would improve the group's process.
questions.answer: A strong response identifies specific behaviors such as questioning evidence, acknowledging concerns, interrupting, relying on assumptions, or pressuring others. It explains the consequences of those behaviors and proposes a relevant, actionable norm.
questions.rationale: Connects interpretation of a text with analysis of collaborative practices.

questions.prompt: In a group of three or four, investigate a debatable literary, cultural, or school-related question. Before meeting, each student must prepare at least two relevant sources or passages, an initial interpretation, and two inquiry questions. Establish written group norms, a shared goal, responsibilities, and a timeline. Conduct and document at least two collaborative discussions, consider competing interpretations or solutions, provide feedback, and produce a coherent 600–800-word analytical report or equivalent multimodal product. Each member must submit an individual preparation record, contribution log, and 250-word reflection evaluating the group's process and personal contributions.
questions.answer: Evaluate individual preparation, the quality of group norms and procedures, meaningful participation, active listening, evidence-based exchange, constructive feedback, shared inquiry, the coherence of the final product, and thoughtful individual reflection. Use individual evidence of contribution alongside the group product.
questions.rationale: Integrates all four expectations through authentic collaborative inquiry, shared production, and individual accountability.

evidence: An individual discussion preparation sheet containing claims, evidence, and questions.
A collaboratively developed group charter establishing norms, goals, and procedures.
A project plan documenting responsibilities, milestones, and progress.
Teacher observation notes or a discussion transcript showing contributions and responses to peers.
An evidence-based group interpretation or inquiry summary.
Peer feedback demonstrating specific, constructive responses to others' work.
A collaboratively created literary, informational, or multimodal text.
Individual contribution records documenting preparation and participation.
A reflection identifying effective group practices and needed improvements.
instruction: Teach collaboration explicitly rather than assuming students already know how to work productively in groups.
Distinguish collaboration from dividing a project into unrelated individual tasks.
Require manageable individual preparation before collaborative discussions.
Model how to establish clear group norms, goals, procedures, and responsibilities.
Use authentic interpretive questions that benefit from considering multiple perspectives.
Teach active listening through paraphrasing, clarifying questions, and accurate acknowledgment of others' ideas.
Provide sentence stems for respectful disagreement and evidence-based response.
Use structured discussion protocols initially, then gradually increase student responsibility for managing the process.
Rotate facilitation and other responsibilities so students practice different collaborative skills.
Teach students to provide feedback that identifies a specific strength, concern, or possible improvement.
Allow students to revise interpretations when peers present persuasive evidence.
Build checkpoints into extended projects to address problems before deadlines.
Provide multiple participation pathways, including written preparation, small-group dialogue, and shared drafting.
Use individual reflection and contribution evidence to distinguish personal learning from group performance.
Evaluate both the collaborative process and the quality of the resulting inquiry or text.
watchFor: Assuming that placing students in groups automatically creates collaboration.
Equating frequent speaking with meaningful contribution.
Allowing confident speakers to dominate while others have limited opportunities to participate.
Requiring students to agree rather than teaching them to explore evidence-based disagreement.
Treating respectful disagreement as interpersonal conflict.
Using group roles that permanently assign intellectual work to some students and clerical work to others.
Confusing equal participation with identical tasks or identical speaking time.
Grading all members solely on the quality of a shared product.
Failing to establish expectations for preparation and accountability.
Using vague feedback such as 'good job' without specific observations.
Allowing group discussions to drift without a clear inquiry question or goal.
Mistaking a quick consensus for a well-supported conclusion.
Requiring students to disclose personal experiences when a text-based or hypothetical example would serve the same purpose.
Overstructuring discussions so students never learn to manage collaboration independently.
Ignoring accessibility, language needs, or other barriers to participation.
Treating a quiet but prepared and thoughtful participant as automatically disengaged.
Failing to address unequal workloads until the project is complete.
unpackings.readingSelectionNote: Selections are illustrative teacher-developed recommendations, not state-prescribed works. Confirm access, permissions, excerpt length, and age suitability. High Interest and accessibility are editorial judgments rather than validated reading-level measures. Texts about group decision-making can provide valuable models and counterexamples, but the primary evidence for this standard should come from students' actual collaborative preparation, discussions, feedback, inquiry, and shared work. Assess individual participation and growth alongside the quality of group products.

Rehearse and evaluate delivery choices for clarity, engagement, and effectiveness (9.P.CP.2.c).

Ask appropriate questions to clarify audience perspectives or advance dialogue (9.P.CP.2.d).
Study the context, meaning, structure, and language of significant poems or speeches before reciting them (9.P.CP.2.e).
Recite all or part of a significant poem or speech using delivery choices informed by understanding of the text (9.P.CP.2.e).
Use feedback and self-reflection to improve presentation content, format, and delivery (9.P.CP.2.a–e).
targets: I can explain my presentation's purpose and identify its intended audience.
I can organize ideas so listeners can follow my reasoning.
I can present information clearly using relevant details and evidence.
I can choose an appropriate format and combine communication modes purposefully.
I can adjust tone and pace to support meaning.
I can use nonverbal communication appropriately without distracting from my message.
I can listen to audience questions and respond thoughtfully.
I can ask questions that support productive audience dialogue.
I can explain the meaning and context of a significant poem or speech.
I can recite a meaningful passage with interpretation and purposeful delivery.
I can evaluate my presentation and identify specific improvements.

vocabulary.definition: A planned communication of ideas, information, or texts to an audience.
vocabulary.example: A student explains the findings of a literary research project.

vocabulary.definition: The people who receive or participate in a communication.
vocabulary.example: A student adjusts explanations when presenting to incoming ninth graders.

vocabulary.definition: The outcome or effect a communicator intends to accomplish.
vocabulary.example: A presentation seeks to help classmates evaluate competing interpretations of a novel.

vocabulary.definition: A means of communicating meaning, such as linguistic, visual, aural, gestural, or spatial expression.
vocabulary.example: A presentation combines spoken explanation with a labeled diagram.

vocabulary.definition: A recognizable type of communication associated with particular conventions.
vocabulary.example: A literary reading, scientific briefing, and persuasive speech have different expectations.

vocabulary.definition: The attitude communicated through language or delivery.
vocabulary.example: A speaker adopts a measured, serious tone when discussing a sensitive issue.

vocabulary.definition: The rate at which speech is delivered.
vocabulary.example: A presenter slows down while explaining a complex process.

vocabulary.definition: Special attention given to words, phrases, or ideas through delivery.
vocabulary.example: A speaker stresses a key contrast in a sentence.

vocabulary.definition: The clear formation of speech sounds.
vocabulary.example: A presenter practices unfamiliar terminology before a research presentation.

vocabulary.definition: Meaning conveyed through gestures, posture, facial expression, movement, or other nonspoken behavior.
vocabulary.example: A speaker gestures toward a chart when discussing its central finding.

vocabulary.definition: A presentation that combines two or more modes of communication.
vocabulary.example: A student uses narration, images, and on-screen labels in an explanatory video.

vocabulary.definition: An exchange of questions, responses, and ideas between presenter and audience.
vocabulary.example: After presenting an argument, a student considers and answers a classmate's question.

vocabulary.definition: The oral delivery of a poem, speech, or other text, often from memory.
vocabulary.example: A student recites a selected stanza and explains its imagery and historical context.

vocabulary.definition: Speaking choices that communicate an informed understanding of a text.
vocabulary.example: A student uses pauses and emphasis to clarify the contrast between two ideas in a poem.

vocabulary.definition: Purposeful practice intended to improve content, timing, delivery, or confidence.
vocabulary.example: A presenter records a practice speech and revises the pacing.
