differentiation.title: Say it so they understand
differentiation.activity: Students prepare a 60–90-second explanation of a familiar topic using a three-part organizer: main idea, supporting detail, and conclusion. They practice with a partner, focusing on clear organization and purposeful pacing. The listener asks one clarification question, and the presenter responds before making one improvement.
differentiation.scaffolds: Presentation organizer, optional speaking notes, teacher model, rehearsal partner, question stems.
differentiation.success: Communicate a clear central idea, include relevant support, make one purposeful delivery choice, and answer an audience question.
differentiation.materials: Planning organizer; speaking notes; simple feedback checklist.

differentiation.title: Poetry in performance
differentiation.activity: Students study a significant poem or excerpt, examining its context, meaning, syntax, sound, and rhetorical choices. They annotate intended pauses, emphasis, and tone, then rehearse and recite all or part of the poem. Afterward, students explain two interpretive delivery decisions and answer a question about the text.
differentiation.scaffolds: Annotated model, historical context notes, audio example, rehearsal opportunities, optional small-group performance.
differentiation.success: Demonstrate accurate understanding of the passage, purposeful interpretive delivery, and the ability to explain choices using textual evidence.
differentiation.materials: Authorized poem or excerpt; annotation sheet; rehearsal and reflection rubric.

differentiation.title: The public humanities talk
differentiation.activity: Students develop a 4–6-minute presentation exploring a meaningful literary or cultural question for an authentic audience. They establish a focused interpretation, research relevant context, integrate appropriate modes, and plan purposeful delivery. Each presentation includes a brief recitation of a significant poem or speech excerpt connected to the topic, followed by audience questions. Students submit a reflection analyzing their content, delivery, and responses.
differentiation.scaffolds: Optional presentation storyboard, source evaluation guide, rehearsal conference, accessibility checklist, question-and-answer planning sheet.
differentiation.success: Deliver a coherent, well-supported, audience-centered presentation with purposeful multimodal choices, informed recitation, effective delivery, and thoughtful audience dialogue.
differentiation.materials: Credible sources; authorized literary excerpt; presentation tools; audience feedback and reflection forms.

questions.prompt: A student must explain a complex scientific process to classmates unfamiliar with the topic. Which presentation strategy best serves the audience?
options: Use technical terminology without explanation.
Speak quickly so every detail fits into the allotted time.
Introduce key terms, organize the process into stages, and use a clearly labeled diagram.
Display a large block of text and read every sentence aloud.
questions.answer: Introduce key terms, organize the process into stages, and use a clearly labeled diagram.
questions.rationale: The strategy supports clear communication and integrates a useful visual mode appropriate to the audience.

questions.prompt: A presenter reaches an especially important conclusion. Which delivery decision is most likely to emphasize it effectively?
options: Maintain the same rapid pace throughout the presentation.
Pause briefly before the conclusion and deliver it at a deliberate pace.
Turn away from the audience and lower the voice until the words are inaudible.
Add unrelated gestures to every word.
questions.answer: Pause briefly before the conclusion and deliver it at a deliberate pace.
questions.rationale: A purposeful pause and controlled pacing can direct audience attention toward an important idea.

questions.prompt: An audience member asks a question that the presenter cannot answer confidently. What is the strongest response?
options: Invent an answer to avoid appearing uncertain.
Ignore the question and immediately end the presentation.
Acknowledge the uncertainty, explain what is known, and identify how the question could be investigated.
Criticize the audience member for asking.
questions.answer: Acknowledge the uncertainty, explain what is known, and identify how the question could be investigated.
questions.rationale: Responsible audience dialogue values accuracy, respectful engagement, and thoughtful responses.

questions.prompt: A student will present the same research findings to classmates and to a school board committee. Explain two ways the presentation might appropriately change while preserving the accuracy of the findings.
questions.answer: A strong response might explain that the student could adjust the amount of background information, examples, terminology, tone, organization, or visual support. Each change should be connected to the needs and purpose of the particular audience.
questions.rationale: Assesses audience-centered choices about clarity, modes, genre, and delivery.

questions.prompt: Select a significant poem or speech excerpt appropriate to Grade 9. Explain its context and central meaning. Annotate the passage to indicate at least three planned delivery choices, such as pauses, emphasis, tone, or pace. Recite the passage and explain how two choices communicate your interpretation.
questions.answer: Evaluate accurate contextual understanding, evidence-based interpretation, preparation, purposeful delivery, and the student's ability to explain how the recitation communicates meaning. Where memory is part of the task, assess it separately from interpretation and delivery.
questions.rationale: Directly addresses the standard's recitation expectation while connecting performance to textual understanding.

questions.prompt: Prepare a 4–6-minute presentation answering a literary or cultural inquiry question. Define your audience and purpose, develop a clear central idea, and support it with evidence from at least two credible sources or relevant texts. Integrate an appropriate visual, audio, or other supporting mode. Include an informed recitation of all or part of a significant poem or speech related to your inquiry. Rehearse tone, pacing, and nonverbal communication. After presenting, ask or invite at least two audience questions and respond thoughtfully. Submit a 300-word reflection evaluating your communication choices, recitation, and audience dialogue.
questions.answer: Evaluate clarity and organization, accuracy and relevance of evidence, appropriateness of presentation modes, purposeful delivery, understanding demonstrated through recitation, responsiveness to questions, and quality of reflection. Provide accessible alternatives for students whose communication needs require them.
questions.rationale: Integrates all five expectations through research-based presentation, multimodal communication, interpretive recitation, audience interaction, and reflection.

evidence: A presentation plan identifying audience, purpose, central idea, and supporting evidence.
A storyboard or outline showing purposeful organization and integration of presentation modes.
An annotated rehearsal script marking tone, pace, emphasis, or nonverbal choices.
A live or recorded presentation demonstrating clear communication.
An annotated significant poem or speech excerpt showing understanding and planned recitation.
A recitation demonstrating interpretive delivery informed by textual analysis.
Audience questions and presenter responses demonstrating thoughtful dialogue.
Peer or teacher feedback identifying specific strengths and improvements.
A self-assessment comparing intended communication effects with audience feedback.
A revision or reflection explaining changes made after rehearsal or presentation.
instruction: Teach presentation as a combination of ideas, audience awareness, format, delivery, and dialogue.
Begin with short, low-stakes speaking opportunities before assigning extended presentations.
Model how to establish a clear central idea and organize information for listeners.
Teach students to select evidence and examples appropriate to their audience's prior knowledge.
Compare presentations from different genres, such as literary readings, research briefings, and persuasive talks.
Demonstrate when visuals, audio, demonstrations, or other modes meaningfully support a message.
Discourage slides filled with text that the presenter simply reads aloud.
Teach tone and pace through comparison of different deliveries of the same short passage.
Use rehearsal recordings or peer observations to help students notice delivery patterns.
Discuss nonverbal communication as context-dependent rather than requiring one universal performance style.
Teach strategies for listening to questions, clarifying their meaning, and responding with evidence.
Model how to acknowledge uncertainty or respectfully address disagreement.
Provide historical and literary context before asking students to recite significant poetry or speeches.
Use close reading and annotation to connect recitation choices with meaning, sound, and rhetorical structure.
Provide students with opportunities to practice, receive feedback, and improve before high-stakes assessment.
Include captions, readable visuals, accessible materials, and appropriate communication accommodations.
Evaluate content, delivery, recitation, and audience dialogue through clearly distinguished criteria.
watchFor: Equating presentation quality with confidence, extroversion, or charisma.
Rewarding volume or theatricality more than clarity and meaning.
Treating eye contact as a universal requirement for effective communication.
Assuming gestures and facial expressions carry identical meanings across cultures and individuals.
Penalizing students for disability-related or language-related differences unrelated to the learning target.
Allowing decorative slides or effects to substitute for accurate content.
Using visuals that are unreadable, unexplained, or inaccessible.
Speaking too quickly to accommodate excessive information.
Assuming slower speech is always better regardless of context.
Memorizing a presentation without understanding its content.
Treating recitation as a memory test disconnected from literary or rhetorical interpretation.
Requiring students to imitate a single supposedly correct performance of a poem.
Selecting significant speeches or poems without teaching their historical or cultural context.
Ignoring copyright or performance permissions when recording or distributing recitations.
Answering audience questions with unsupported claims or invented information.
Treating audience questions as interruptions rather than opportunities for dialogue.
Assessing only the finished presentation without providing opportunities for rehearsal and revision.
Combining all presentation criteria into one vague score that obscures students' strengths and needs.
unpackings.readingSelectionNote: Selections are illustrative teacher-developed recommendations, not state-prescribed works. Confirm access, permissions, excerpt length, age suitability, and any recording or performance restrictions. High Interest and accessibility are editorial judgments rather than validated reading-level measures. Expectation 9.P.CP.2.e explicitly includes recitation of significant poems and speeches; include meaningful recitation in instruction and assessment rather than treating it as optional enrichment. Support varied communication styles and accessibility needs while maintaining the standard's emphasis on purposeful, clear presentation and audience dialogue.
